<!-- head-1: body_md -->
\emph{Let $G/K$ be a compact Hermitian symmetric
space of complex dimension $n$, and let $E_\nu$ be a one-dimensional
admissible twist. A pair $(\psi,A)$ satisfying
$F_{A}^-=0$ is an absolute minimum of the energy functional $\mathcal{E}_{{|}_{\mathcal{C}_{SD}}}$ if
\begin{equation} 
  D_{A}^+\psi=0,\qquad
  F_{A}^+=-\frac{a_n}{8}\sigma(\psi)^+,\qquad
  \Lambda_\omega F_{A}\ \text{is constant}.
  \label{eq:theorem-a-intro}
\end{equation}
The last condition in \eqref{eq:theorem-a-intro} is vacuous when $n=2$ and is automatic when $A\in\mathcal A^G$. We equip $G/K$ with a Riemannian metric corresponding to $\lambda {B_{\mathfrak g}}_{{|}_{\mathfrak p}}$, where $B_{\mathfrak g}$ is the Killing form and $\lambda$ is a negative real parameter. For an invariant connection, the
$\zeta$-perturbed monopole equation for $\zeta=it\omega$, where $t$ is a real parameter, is equivalent to
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}(n-4k)
       |\psi^{(2k)}|^2=c_n(t,\nu,\lambda),\qquad
 \langle\gamma(\eta_{ij})\psi,\psi\rangle
 =\langle\gamma(\theta_{ij})\psi,\psi\rangle=0,
 \label{eq:explicit-monopole-intro}
\end{equation}
where
\[ c_n(t,\nu,\lambda)=8n\left(t+\frac{\nu}{2\lambda}\right).\]
}
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- head-2: body_md -->
\emph{Let $G/K$ be irreducible of complex dimension $n$, let $E_\nu$ be a
one-dimensional admissible twist, and let $A\in\mathcal A^G$. If $G$ is
compact, then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal M^\infty_{\nu,{eq}}(c_n)\cong
 \begin{cases}
   \{\mathrm{pt}\},&
       c_n>0,\ \nu=1,\\
   \{\mathrm{reducible\ pt}\},&
       c_n=0,\ \text{for every admissible }\nu,\\
   \{\mathrm{pt}\},&
       c_n<0,\ \nu=-1,\ n\ \text{even},\\
   \varnothing,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
 \label{eq:theorem-b-intro}
\end{equation}
If $G$ is non-compact, then
$\mathcal M^{L^2}_{\nu,\mathrm{eq}}(c_n)$ is the reducible point when $c_n=0$ and
is empty otherwise.
}
<!-- end head-2 -->
<!-- head-3: body_md -->
\emph{Let $G/K$ be an irreducible Hermitian symmetric space of complex
dimension $n$. If $G$ is compact and $\nu\leq-1$, there is a unique
$w\in W_G$ for which
\[
  w(\nu\rho_{\mathfrak p}+\rho_{\mathfrak k})
       -\rho_{\mathfrak g}
\]
is dominant, and $\ell(w)=n$. Consequently,
\[
  \ker D^+(E_\nu)\neq0
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n\in2\mathbb Z.
\]
For $\nu\geq1$, the non-triviality holds unconditionally. If $G$ is non-compact, $\nu\geq1$, and
$\delta_\nu:=\nu\rho_{\mathfrak p}+\rho_{\mathfrak k}$, then
\[
  \ker_{L^2}D^+(E_{\nu\rho_{\mathfrak p}})
  \ \text{is a discrete-series representation}
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n\in2\mathbb Z.
\]
Whenever it occurs, its Harish--Chandra parameter is $\delta_\nu$;  for $\nu\leq -1$, this holds unconditionally. For
$|\nu|<1$, both non-triviality and the discrete-series realisation fail.
}
<!-- end head-3 -->
<!-- head-4: body_md -->
\emph{Let $M=G/K$ be compact and irreducible, let $E_\nu$ be a one-dimensional admissible twist and let $\mu=\deg_\omega(\mathcal{E}_{\nu-1})$, $\nu\geq 1$. Then
\begin{equation}
 \bigl(\mathcal M_\nu^\infty(c_n)\bigr)^G\cong
 \begin{cases}
   \bigl(\operatorname{Div}^{\mu}_+(M)\bigr)^G,&c_n>0,\\
   \bigl(\operatorname{Hol}^{\mu}(M)\bigr)^G,&c_n=0,\\
   \varnothing,&c_n<0.
 \end{cases}
 \label{eq:theorem-d-intro}
\end{equation}}
<!-- end head-4 -->
<!-- convention--1: body_md -->
\label{conventionHSS} $ $
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)] From \cref{subsec:HSS} onwards, $G$ is a connected simple Lie group with finite center and $K$ is a subgroup with one-dimensional center,                                                                                                
    so that $G/K$ is an irreducible Hermitian symmetric space. The reductive notation ${\mathfrak g}={\mathfrak h}\,\oplus\,{\mathfrak q}$ is used only in \cref{wang} and \cref{subsec:dirac}; everywhere else ${\mathfrak h}={\mathfrak k}$ and ${\mathfrak q}={\mathfrak p}$.
    \item[(ii)] We fix the Cartan subalgebra $i{\mathfrak t}$, where ${\mathfrak t}$ is a maximal abelian subalgebra of ${\mathfrak k}$. Positive roots are chosen so that ${\mathfrak p}^{\pm}_{\mathbb{C}}=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Delta^{+}_{{\mathfrak p}}}{\mathfrak g}_{\pm\alpha}$ are the $\pm i$-eigenspaces of $J$, see \cite{Kna96} for reference.                                                                                                                                                                      
    \item[(iii)] Sections of vector-valued forms of homogeneous bundles are occasionally expressed in the form $f^{ij}\otimes u_i\otimes v_j$, as elements of $\{C^\infty(G)\otimes U\otimes V\}^K$.
    \item[(iv)] On endomorphisms we use the norm induced by the Hilbert--Schmidt inner product $\langle A,B\rangle=\ensuremath{\mathrm{tr}}(B^*A)$.
                                                                                                                                                                                                          
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end convention--1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{Brad1} Let $(M,\omega)$ be a closed Kähler manifold and $\mu$ a non-negative integer. Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Div}\,}_+^\mu(M)$ be the set of effective divisors with degree $\deg_\omega$ equal to $\mu$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Hol}\,}^\mu(M)$ the set of holomorphic line bundles of degree $\mu$.
We fix $t$ and set $b(\mu,t)=t-4\pi\mu/{\mathrm{vol}}(M)$. 
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal{M}_t^\mu\cong
 \begin{cases}
   \ensuremath{\mathrm{Div}\,}_+^{\mu}(M),&b(\mu,t)>0,\\
   \ensuremath{\mathrm{Hol}\,}^{\mu}(M),&b(\mu,t)=0,\\
   \varnothing,&b(\mu,t)<0.
 \end{cases}
 \end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:signlambda}
For $(\cdot,\cdot)_{{\mathfrak q},\lambda}$ to be positive definite, $\lambda$ must be negative
when $G$ is compact and positive when $G$ is non-compact. This is the criterion by
which the two cases are distinguished throughout.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{FAabelian}
At any other point $p$, ${F_{A}}_p$ is given by the image of ${F_{A}}_{p_0}$ under the adjoint action of the Lie group $F$. If $F$ is the abelian $U(1)$, the curvature of an invariant connection is therefore constant.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{Z_0*rho}
If $Z_{0}^*\in{\mathfrak z}_{{\mathfrak k}}^*$ denotes the dual of $Z_{0}$, then $iZ^{*}_{0}=\tfrac2n\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}$. In particular, $\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}\perp\Delta_{\mathfrak k}$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Follows directly from \cref{aZ0} and the table above.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{omegavarpirel}
We consider the K\"ahler form $\omega_\lambda(X,Y)=\lambda B_{{\mathfrak p}}(JX,Y)$. For all $X,Y\in{\mathfrak p}$, 
\[\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}\bigl([X,Y]\bigr)=-\frac{i}{4\lambda}\,\omega_\lambda(X,Y)
\qquad\iff \quad \omega_\lambda(X,Y)=2\lambda N i\,\varpi_{{\mathfrak p}}(\text{ad}(X)Y).\]
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
By \cref{Z_0*rho} and $B_{{\mathfrak g}}(Z_0,Z_0)=-2n$, we have $\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}([X,Y])=-\tfrac{i}{4}B_{{\mathfrak g}}([X,Y],Z_{0})$. The Killing form is invariant under the adjoint action, thus $B_{{\mathfrak g}}([X,Y],Z_{0})=B_{{\mathfrak g}}(JX,Y)=B_{{\mathfrak p}}(JX,Y)$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{LiftTable}
    Let $\xi\in \mathbb{Q}$, $o(\cdot)$ denote the order of an element, and let $\ell =\big |(Z(K))_0\, \cap \, K_{ss}\big|$, where $K_{ss}=[K,K]$. Then $\xi\rho_{\mathfrak p}$                                                                                                 
    lifts to $K$ if and only if $(\xi n  o(e^{2\pi Z_0}))/(2\ell)$ is an integer.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                
Explicitly, the character $\chi_{\xi\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}}$ lifts to $K$ precisely under the following conditions. The table reads $\xi N/2\in\mathbb{Z}$ in all types except D\textsubscript{III}, where it reads $\xi N/4\in\mathbb{Z}$.
\begin{table}[h]
\begingroup
\small
\begin{center}
\renewcommand{1.3}{1.4}
\begin{NiceTabular}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c}[hvlines]
\textbf{Type} & A\textsubscript{III} & BD\textsubscript{I} & D\textsubscript{III} & C\textsubscript{I}  & E\textsubscript{III} & E\textsubscript{VII} \\
\textbf{Condition} & ${\tfrac{\xi  (p+q)}{2}\in \mathbb{Z}}$ & ${\tfrac{\xi p}{2}\in \mathbb{Z}}$ & ${\tfrac{\xi (p-1)}{2}\in \mathbb{Z}}$ & ${\tfrac{\xi (p+1)}{2}\in \mathbb{Z}}$ & $6\xi\in \mathbb{Z}$ & $9\xi\in \mathbb{Z}$ 
\end{NiceTabular}
\end{center}
\endgroup
\vspace{-1mm}
\end{table}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
According to \cite{Kna96} Proposition 4.58, a linear form $\zeta$ lifts to the identity component $(Z(K))_0$ if and only if $\zeta(Z)\in 2\pi i\mathbb{Z}$ for all $Z\in \exp^{-1}(1_{(Z(K))_0})$. By Theorem 4.29 of the same reference, $K=(Z_{K})_0 K_{ss}$. Therefore every such element $Z$ is of the form $\kappa 2\pi Z_0 \, o(e^{2\pi Z_0})/\ell$, where $\kappa$ is an integer. From \cref{Z_0*rho}, $\xi\rho_{\mathfrak p}$ lifts if and only if
    \begin{align*}
        \xi\rho_{\mathfrak p}\left(\kappa 2\pi Z_0 \, o(e^{2\pi Z_0})/\ell\right)\in 2\pi i\mathbb{Z} \iff  (\xi n  o(e^{2\pi Z_0}) )/(2\ell)\in \mathbb{Z}.
    \end{align*}
 To obtain the stated criterion, we substitute the following data in each case.
    \begin{center}
    \small
\renewcommand{1.3}{1.2}
\begin{NiceTabular}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}[hlines]
\textbf{Type} & A\textsubscript{III} & BD\textsubscript{I} & D\textsubscript{III} & C\textsubscript{I}  & E\textsubscript{III} & E\textsubscript{VII}\\
${o(e^{2\pi Z_0})}$ & ${\tfrac{p+q}{gcd(p,q)}} $ & $1$ & $2$ & $2$  & $3$ & $2$\\
${(Z(K))_0 \, \cap K_{ss}}$  
& ${\mathbb{Z}_{lcm(p,q)}}$ & ${\{I_{2+ p}\}}$ & ${\mathbb{Z}_p }$ & ${\mathbb{Z}_p}$ & ${\mathbb{Z}_4}$ & ${\mathbb{Z}_3}$\\
\end{NiceTabular}
\end{center}
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{spinrepformula}
    The spin representation is given by the following formulas.
    \begin{align*}
	    sp(Y)=\sum_{\alpha_j>0}\alpha_j(Y)\left(\frac{1}{2}\gamma(X_{\alpha_j}^*)\gamma(X_{-\alpha_j}^*)+\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{id}\right),\ Y\in{\mathfrak t}, \quad sp(Y)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i<j}([Y,X_i],X_j)_{\lambda}\gamma(X_i^*)\gamma(X_j^*), \ Y\in {\mathfrak k}.
	\end{align*}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{uweights}
        The vector ${u_I=X_{-\alpha_{i_1}}^*\wedge \cdots \wedge X_{-\alpha_{i_s}}^*, \, I=\{ 1\leq i_1<\cdots<i_s \leq n\}}$, where ${u_{\varnothing}\coloneqq 1}$, is a ${\mathfrak t}_{\mathfrak k}$-vector of weight 
        \[ {-\rho_{\mathfrak g}+\rho_{\mathfrak k}+\sum_{j\in I}\alpha_j=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j\in I}\alpha_j-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j\notin I}\alpha_j}.\]
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:weights}
The vectors $u_{\varnothing}$ and $u_{\mathrm{top}}$ have weights $-\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}$ and $\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{sptraceless}
For $n\ne1$ the representations $\ensuremath{\mathrm{sp\,}}^{(\pm)}$ are traceless. For $n=1$ the representation $\ensuremath{\mathrm{sp\,}}$ is traceless while $\ensuremath{\mathrm{tr}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{sp\,}}^{\pm})=\mp\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{admissibledef}
A finite-dimensional irreducible ${\mathfrak k}$-representation $(E_{\nu},\pi_{\nu})$ is an \emph{admissible twist} if $(S\otimes E_{\nu},\ensuremath{\mathrm{sp\,}}\otimes\pi_{\nu})$
lifts to a representation $\beta^{\nu}$ of $K$, that is, $d\beta^{\nu}=\ensuremath{\mathrm{sp\,}}\otimes\pi_{\nu}$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{Liftinglemma}
If $S^{(\pm)}$ does not lift to $K$, there exists a one-dimensional admissible twist $E_{\nu}:=E_{\nu\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}}$. Every such twist has $\nu=1+2\kappa/N$, with $\kappa\in2\mathbb{Z}$ if $G/K$ is of type D\textsubscript{III} and $\kappa\in\mathbb{Z}$ otherwise.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
From \cite{Kna86}, $S\simeq\Lambda{\mathfrak p}^{+}\otimes(\Lambda^{\mathrm{top}}{\mathfrak p}^{-})^{1/2}$ with ${\mathfrak k}$ acting by the adjoint action on each factor. The first factor lifts to $K$ because ${\mathfrak p}^{+}$ does. If $(\Lambda^{\mathrm{top}}{\mathfrak p}^{-})^{1/2}=\mathbb{C}_{-\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}}$ does not lift, consider a one-dimensional ${\mathfrak k}$-representation $E_{\chi}=V_{0}\otimes\mathbb{C}_{\chi}$ with $V_{0}$ trivial on ${\mathfrak k}_{ss}$. Since ${\mathfrak z}_{{\mathfrak k}}$ is one-dimensional, $\chi=\nu\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}$ for some $\nu\in\mathbb{R}$. By \cref{LiftTable} there is always $\nu\in\mathbb{Q}$ for which $\mathbb{C}_{-\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}}\otimes E_{\nu\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}}\simeq\mathbb{C}_{(-1+\nu)\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}}$ lifts to $K$, namely $\nu=1+2\kappa/N$ with $\kappa$ as stated. The same argument applies to $S^{(\pm)}$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:su3}
Here ${\mathfrak k}=\mathfrak{s}({\mathfrak u}(2)\oplus{\mathfrak u}(1))$ and $Z_{0}=\ensuremath{\mathrm{diag}}(i/3,i/3,-2i/3)$. The lexicographic ordering with respect to $\{H_{1}=-iZ_{0},H_{2}=i\,\ensuremath{\mathrm{diag}}(-i,i,0)\}$ gives $\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_1>\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_{2}>\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_{3}$, so
$\Delta_{\mathfrak p}^{+}=\{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_{1}-\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_{3},\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_{2}-\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_{3}\}$,
$\Delta_{\mathfrak k}^{+}=\{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_{1}-\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_{2}\}$ and
$\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_{1}+\tfrac{1}{2}\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_{2}-\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_{3}$. Then, writing $S_{j}=S_{ss}^{j}\otimes S_{{\mathfrak z}_{\mathfrak k}}^{j}$ for an irreducible summand
\[
S=V_{0}\otimes\mathbb{C}_{-\rho_{\mathfrak p}}\oplus V_{1/2(\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_1-\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_2)}\otimes\mathbb{C}_{0}\oplus V_{0}\otimes\mathbb{C}_{\rho_{\mathfrak p}}
\simeq\bigl(V_{0}\otimes\mathbb{C}_{0}\oplus V_{1/2(\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_1-\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_2)}\otimes\mathbb{C}_{\rho_{\mathfrak p}}\oplus V_{0}\otimes\mathbb{C}_{2\rho_{\mathfrak p}}\bigr)\otimes\mathbb{C}_{-\rho_{\mathfrak p}},
\]
and $E_{\nu}$ is admissible if and only if $\nu=1+2\kappa/3$, $\kappa\in\mathbb{Z}$. Analogous decompositions for $\ensuremath{\mathfrak{so}}(5)$ and $\ensuremath{\mathfrak{so}}(6)$, as well as their non-compact duals,                                                                   
are recorded in \cref{exatable}.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:liftfails}
Liftability is not detected factor-wise: if $S_{ss}$ lifts to $K_{ss}$ and $S_{{\mathfrak z}_{{\mathfrak k}}}$ lifts to $K$, then $S_{ss}\otimes S_{{\mathfrak z}_{{\mathfrak k}}}$ lifts to $K$, but the converse fails. For example, if ${\mathfrak g}=\ensuremath{\mathfrak{su}}(3)$ the summand $V_{1}\otimes\mathbb{C}_{\rho_{\mathfrak p}}$ lifts although $\mathbb{C}_{\rho_{\mathfrak p}}$ does not. Likewise, $S^{(\pm)}\otimes E_{\nu}$ may lift to $K$, while neither factor does. For example, if ${\mathfrak g}=\ensuremath{\mathfrak{so}}(5)$ this happens for every admissible $\nu=1+2\kappa/3$.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{2nu}
If $(E_{\nu},\pi_{\nu})$ is a one-dimensional admissible twist, then
$(E_{\nu}\otimes E_{\nu},\pi_{\nu}\otimes\pi_{\nu})$ lifts to $K$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
If $\mathbb{C}_{(-1+\nu)\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}}$ lifts, then $\nu-1$ satisfies the condition of \cref{LiftTable}, which in all types has the form $\xi \ell /2\in\mathbb{Z}$ for a fixed
integer $\ell$; $\ell$ is $N\in\mathbb{Z} $ for all types except D\textsubscript{III}, where $\ell=N/2=p-1\in\mathbb{Z}$. Since $(\nu-1)\ell/2=k\in\mathbb{Z}$ then $\nu=(2k+\ell)/\ell$ and
$2\nu\ell/2=2k+\ell\in\mathbb{Z}$, so $2\nu$ satisfies the same condition.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{detnu}
Let $(E_{\nu},\pi_{\nu})$ be a one-dimensional admissible twist.                                                   
For $n\neq 1$, $\pi_{\nu}=\tfrac{1}{m^{(\pm)}}\ensuremath{\mathrm{tr}}\bigl(d\beta^{\nu,(\pm)}\bigr)$. For $n=1$,
$\pi_{\nu}=\tfrac1m\ensuremath{\mathrm{tr}}(d\beta^{\nu})$ and $\pi_{\nu\mp1}=\tfrac{1}{m^{\pm}}\ensuremath{\mathrm{tr}}(d\beta^{\nu,\pm})$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
A weight basis of $S^{(\pm)}\otimes E_{\nu}$ consists of vectors $u\otimes v$ for a fixed $0\ne v\in E_{\nu}$, on which $d\beta^{\nu,(\pm)}(Y)$ acts by
$\ensuremath{\mathrm{sp\,}}^{(\pm)}(Y)u\otimes v+u\otimes\pi_{\nu}(Y)v$. By \cref{sptraceless} the first summand is traceless for $n\ne1$, so the trace is $m^{(\pm)}\pi_{\nu}(Y)$. For $n=1$ the correction is $\mp\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{1-1cor}
Let $\mathfrak{s}_0$ denote the homogeneous $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Spin}}^c$ structure with $\mathcal{K}^*=\mathcal{E}_{2\rho_{\mathfrak p}}$ as its characteristic bundle. Then, with $\kappa\in2\mathbb{Z}$ for type D\textsubscript{III} and $\kappa\in\mathbb{Z}$ otherwise, the assignment
\begin{align*}
    \{ \text{one-dimensional admissible twists }{E_{\nu}}\} & \quad {\longrightarrow} \quad \{ \text{homogeneous $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}$ structures}\}/\sim\\
    {E_\nu, \, \nu=1+2\kappa/N}\hspace{20mm} & \quad \longmapsto \hspace{20mm} {\mathfrak{s}_0\otimes E_{2\kappa/N}}
\end{align*}
is a bijection between one-dimensional admissible twists and homogeneous $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Spin}}^c$ structures up to equivariant isomorphism.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Both sides are torsors over $\mathrm{Hom}(K,U(1))$. For the admissible twists, if $\nu=1+2\kappa/N$ and $\nu'=1+2\kappa'/N$ then $E_{\nu'}=E_{\nu}\otimes E_{\mu}$ with $\mu=2(\kappa'-\kappa)/N$, and by \cref{LiftTable} $E_{\mu}$ lifts, so $\mu\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}$ integrates to an element of $\mathrm{Hom}(K,U(1))$. For the homogeneous $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Spin}}^c$ structures, if $\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{s}'$ are homogeneous with $\mathfrak{s}'=\mathfrak{s}\otimes E$, then $E$ must be homogeneous, hence
$E=G\times_{\chi}\mathbb{C}$ for some $\chi\in\mathrm{Hom}(K,U(1))$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rem:basepoint}
The base point $\mathfrak{s}_{0}$ corresponds to $S\otimes E_{1}$, with which it
shares the characteristic bundle $\mathcal{K}^{*}=E_{2}$. Moreover, when $n=2$ one has $m^{\pm}=2$ and \cref{linebndleequiv} gives $\mathcal{L}_{\nu}\simeq\det(\mathcal{S}^{\pm}\otimes \mathcal{E}_{\nu})$; so $\mathfrak{s}_{0}$ is the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Spin}}^c$ structure with determinant bundle $\mathcal{K}^{*}$, as in the classical formulation.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:trace}
The curvature of the \emph{virtual} connection on $\mathcal{E}_{\nu}$ is the trace of one living on a bundle that always exists. Indeed, for $n\ne1$, \cref{sptraceless} and \cref{eq:Ftwisted} give
\[\frac{1}{m^{(\pm)}}\ensuremath{\mathrm{tr}}\bigl(F_{A_{S^{(\pm)}\otimes E_{\nu}}}\bigr)=-\sum_{i<j}^{2n}1\otimes X^{*}_{i}\wedge X^{*}_{j}\otimes\nu\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}([X_{i},X_{j}]_{{\mathfrak k}})
=F_{A_{{E}_{\nu}}} .
\]
For $n=1$ the same holds for $S$, with $\nu$ replaced by $\nu\mp1$ on $S^{\pm}$.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:Fomega}
Let $E_{\nu}$ be a one-dimensional admissible twist and $A_{E_{\nu}}\in\mathcal{A}^G$. Then
\[
F_{A_{E_{\nu}}}=\frac{\nu i}{4\lambda}\,\omega .
\]
Consequently $\Lambda_{\omega}F_{A_{E_{\nu}}}=\tfrac{n\nu i}{4\lambda}$ is constant.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
By the table above and \cref{omegavarpirel},
$F_{A_{E_{\nu}}}=\tfrac{\nu i}{4\lambda}\sum_{i<j}\omega(X_{i},X_{j})X^{*}_{i}\wedge X^{*}_{j}
=\tfrac{\nu i}{4\lambda}\omega$. The last assertion follows from
$\Lambda_{\omega}\omega=|\omega|^{2}=n$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:kernelrep}
If $A\in\mathcal{A}^G$, then $D_A$ is $G$-equivariant and therefore $\ker D_{A}$ is a $G$-representation.
Conversely, if $D_A$ commutes with the left action of $G$, then the calculation
following \cref{eq:diracgeneric} forces $A\in\mathcal{A}^G$.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rem:D0}
The operator $D_0+D_1$ in \cref{DAsecond} is Kostant's cubic Dirac operator for the pair $({\mathfrak g},{\mathfrak h})$ and $s=1/3$, with cubic term $D_1$, see \cite{Ko99}. On a Hermitian symmetric space, ${\mathfrak h}={\mathfrak k}$, ${\mathfrak q}={\mathfrak p}$ and $[{\mathfrak p},{\mathfrak p}]_{\mathfrak p}=0$ annihilates $D_1$. Also, under the assumption that $E_{\mu}=E_{\nu\rho_{\mathfrak p}}$ is one-dimensional, $D_{2}=0$ by \cref{eq:Lambdavanish}. Hence,
\[D^{\Lambda_{E_{\nu}}}_{s}=D_{0}\] 
for every $s$, and we write $D_{0}$ throughout.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{Y2}
    Let $ {Y\in {\mathfrak k}}$, $ {\psi\in \{ C^{\infty}(G)\otimes S\otimes E_\nu\}^K}$.
    \begin{align*}
         {[2r(Y)\otimes sp(Y)\otimes1]\psi}& {=[-r(Y^2)\otimes 1\otimes1-1\otimes sp(Y^2)\otimes1+1\otimes1\otimes\nu\rho_{\mathfrak p}(Y^2)]\psi}\\
         {[2 (1\otimes sp(Y)\otimes\nu\rho_{\mathfrak p}(Y))]\psi}& {=[-1\otimes sp(Y^2)\otimes1-1\otimes 1\otimes\nu\rho_{\mathfrak p}(Y^2)+r(Y^2)\otimes1\otimes1]\psi}\\
         {[2r(Y)\otimes1\otimes\nu\rho_{\mathfrak p}(Y)]\psi}& {=[-r(Y^2)\otimes 1\otimes1-1\otimes 1\otimes\nu\rho_{\mathfrak p}(Y^2)+1\otimes sp(Y^2)\otimes1]\psi}
    \end{align*}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
We write $a=r(Y)\otimes1\otimes1$, $b=1\otimes\ensuremath{\mathrm{sp\,}}(Y)\otimes1$ and $c=1\otimes1\otimes\nu\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}(Y)$ and we need to show 
\[
2ab\,\psi=(c^{2}-a^{2}-b^{2})\psi,\qquad
2bc\,\psi=(a^{2}-b^{2}-c^{2})\psi,\qquad
2ac\,\psi=(b^{2}-a^{2}-c^{2})\psi .
\]
$K$-invariance of $\psi$ reads exactly $(a+b+c)\psi=0$. Then $(a+b)^{2}\psi=c^{2}\psi$, and expanding gives the first identity. The other two follow by symmetry.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{Dsquare}
    The square of the operator $ {D_0}$ applied on $ {\psi\in \{ C^{\infty}(G)\otimes S\otimes E_\nu\}^K}$ is given by 
     \[ {D_0^2 \psi=\left[-r(\Omega_{{\mathfrak p}})\otimes 1\otimes 1 +\frac{\ensuremath{\mathrm{scal\,}}(\lambda)}{4}\cdot 1\otimes 1\otimes1-\sum_{1\leq i<j \leq 2n}1\otimes \gamma(X_i^*)\gamma(X_j^*)\otimes \nu\rho_{\mathfrak p}([X_i,X_j])\right]\psi}.\]
and the last term is $\gamma\bigl(F_{A_{\mathcal{E}_{\nu}}}\bigr)$.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
We prove the case of $G$ non-compact; the compact case is handled by analogous
arguments. Since $\gamma(X^{*}_{i})^{2}=-\mathrm{Id}$ and
$\gamma(X^{*}_{i})\gamma(X^{*}_{j})=-\gamma(X^{*}_{j})\gamma(X^{*}_{i})$,
\[
\Bigl(\sum_{i}r(X_{i})\otimes\gamma(X^{*}_{i})\otimes1\Bigr)^{2}
=-r(\Omega_{{\mathfrak p}})\otimes1\otimes1
+\underbrace{\sum_{i<j}^{2n}r([X_{i},X_{j}])\otimes\gamma(X^{*}_{i})\gamma(X^{*}_{j})\otimes1}_{(*)} .
\]
Choose a basis $\{Y_{t}\}$ of ${\mathfrak k}$ with $(Y_{i},Y_{j})_{\lambda}=-\delta_{ij}$, so
$[X_{i},X_{j}]=-\sum_{t}([X_{i},X_{j}],Y_{t})_{\lambda}Y_{t}$. By
\cref{spinrepformula} and $\text{ad}$-invariance,
$(*)=-2\sum_{t}r(Y_{t})\otimes\ensuremath{\mathrm{sp\,}}(Y_{t})\otimes1$. Applying the first identity of
\cref{Y2} and then the second,
\[
(*)=-2\bigl(1\otimes\ensuremath{\mathrm{sp\,}}(\Omega_{{\mathfrak k}})\otimes1\bigr)
-\sum_{i<j}^{2n}1\otimes\gamma(X_i^{*})\gamma(X_j^{*})\otimes\nu\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}([X_{i},X_{j}]).
\]
Finally, since $\gamma(X_i^{*})\gamma(X_j^{*})\gamma(X_i^{*})\gamma(X_j^{*})=-1$
for $i\neq j$, the image of the Casimir simplifies to
\[\ensuremath{\mathrm{sp\,}}(\Omega_{{\mathfrak k}})=-\frac{1}{4}\sum_{i<j}\bigl([X_{i},X_{j}],[X_{i},X_{j}]\bigr)_{\lambda},
\]
which by \cref{eq:scal2} equals $-\tfrac{1}{8}\ensuremath{\mathrm{scal\,}}(\lambda)$, hence
$-2\ensuremath{\mathrm{sp\,}}(\Omega_{{\mathfrak k}})=\tfrac{\ensuremath{\mathrm{scal\,}}(\lambda)}{4}$. The identification of the remaining term with $\gamma(F_{A_{\mathcal{E}_{\nu}}})$ is the first row of the table in \cref{subsec:curvature}.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
(Lichnerowicz formula)\label{Dsquare+} For a four-dimensional Hermitian symmetric space, 
\begin{align}
    {D_0^2\big|\{ C^{\infty}(G)\otimes S^{+}\otimes E_\nu\}^K}&={D_0^+}^*{{D_0}^+} =-{r\left(\Omega_{\mathfrak p} \right)\otimes 1\otimes 1+\tfrac{\ensuremath{\mathrm{scal\,}}}{4}\cdot 1\otimes 1\otimes1+\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}({F_{A^{E_\nu}}}^+}).
\end{align}
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:flat}
Let $\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{flat}}\subseteq\mathcal{A}^G$ denote the invariant flat connections on $\mathcal{E}_{\nu}$. Then $\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{flat}}\neq\varnothing$ if and only if $\nu=0$. The value $\nu=0$ is admissible always in types E\textsubscript{III} and E\textsubscript{VII}, and in the remaining cases, the following criterion must be satisfied.
    \[\begin{NiceTabular}{c|c|c|c|}[hvlines]
    \renewcommand{1.3}{1.3}
A\textsubscript{III} & BD\textsubscript{I} & D\textsubscript{III} & C\textsubscript{I}  \\
${(p+q)/2\in \mathbb{Z}}$ & ${p/2\in \mathbb{Z}}$ & ${(p-1)/2\in \mathbb{Z}}$ & ${(p+1)/2\in \mathbb{Z}}$ 
\end{NiceTabular}\]
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
By \cref{lem:Fomega}, $F_{A_{E_{\nu}}}=\tfrac{\nu i}{4\lambda}\omega$ vanishes if and only if $\nu=0$. Admissibility of $\nu=0$ means $-\rho_{\mathfrak p}$ satisfies the criterion of \cref{LiftTable}, which gives the stated conditions.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lib1}\label{lib2} For ${\beta, \, \beta_1,\, \beta_2 \in\Lambda^{k}{\mathfrak p}_\mathbb{C}^{*}}$,
        \begin{equation*}
        \begin{array}{cccccc}
           { (i)}&{\ \tau (\Omega)=\Omega} & { (ii)}&{ (\tau \beta_1,\tau \beta_2)_{\tau }=\tau(\beta_1,\beta_2)_{\tau }} & { (iii)}&{*\tau (\beta)=\tau (*\beta)}\\
           {(iv)}&{ **\beta=(-1)^{k(2n-k)}\beta} & { (v)}&{\ \beta_1\wedge *\tau (\beta_2)=( \beta_1,\beta_2)_{\tau} \Omega} &  {( vi)}&{ (*\beta_1,*\beta_2)_{\tau}=(\beta_1,\beta_2)_{\tau}}
           \end{array}
        \end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{Phi}
Let $G/K$ be a Hermitian symmetric space and of complex dimension $n\geq 2$. 
\[\Phi:=\frac{\omega^{n-2}}{(n-2)!} \quad \text{ admits the expression }\quad\Phi=i^{\,n-2}\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n}
\bigwedge_{\substack{1\leq k\leq n\\ k\notin\{i,j\}}}
\left(X_{\alpha_k}^{*}\wedge X_{-\alpha_k}^{*}\right)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           
\]
and it is a $K$-invariant $(2n-4)$-form.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The $K$-invariance follows from the invariance of $\omega$. The formula follows by direct computation.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:twistedhodge}
Let $G/K$ be a Hermitian symmetric space and $\Phi$ the $K$-invariant $(2n-4)$-form of \cref{Phi}. The \emph{twisted Hodge operator} is
\[*_{\Phi}\colon\Lambda^{2}{\mathfrak p}^{*}_{\mathbb{C}}\to\Lambda^{2}{\mathfrak p}^{*}_{\mathbb{C}}, \qquad \qquad *_{\Phi}\coloneqq *\circ\epsilon(\Phi).\]
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lib4} The twisted Hodge star operator is a $ {K}$-equivariant and $\tau$-equivariant operator.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Immediate from the $ {K},\, \tau$-invariance of $\Phi$ and Lemma \ref{lib2}
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{prop:eigen}
        The twisted Hodge star operator on a Hermitian symmetric space $G/K$ is an involution on $\Lambda^2{\mathfrak p}_\mathbb{C}^*\cap \omega^{\bot}$ and its eigenspace decomposition is 
\[ \Lambda^{2}{\mathfrak p}^{*}_{\mathbb{C}}=V_{+}\oplus V_{-}\oplus\mathbb{C}\omega,\qquad \text{where
}\quad V_{+}=\Lambda^{2}{\mathfrak p}_{\mathbb{C}}^{+\,*}\oplus\Lambda^{2}{\mathfrak p}_{\mathbb{C}}^{-\,*},\qquad
V_{-}=\bigl({\mathfrak p}_\mathbb{C}^{+\,*}\wedge{\mathfrak p}_\mathbb{C}^{-\,*}\bigr)\cap(\mathbb{C}\omega)^{\perp},
\]
The eigenvalues are $+1$, $-1$ and $n-1$ respectively.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Since $X^{*}_{-\alpha_{j}}\wedge X_{\alpha_{j}}^{*}=-X_{\alpha_{j}}^{*}\wedge X^{*}_{-\alpha_{j}}$,
for $\beta=X_{\alpha_{i}}^{*}\wedge X^{*}_{-\alpha_{i}}$ we have $*_{\Phi}\beta=*(\Phi\wedge\beta)=\sum_{j\ne i}X_{\alpha_{j}}^{*}\wedge X^{*}_{-\alpha_{j}}$. Hence, for $\omega=i\sum_{i}X_{\alpha_{i}}^{*}\wedge X^{*}_{-\alpha_{i}}$, we have 
$*_{\Phi}\omega=(n-1)\omega$, while for $i\ne j$,
\[
*_{\Phi}\bigl(X_{\alpha_{i}}^{*}\wedge X^{*}_{-\alpha_{i}}-X_{\alpha_{j}}^{*}\wedge X^{*}_{-\alpha_{j}}\bigr)
=-\bigl(X_{\alpha_{i}}^{*}\wedge X^{*}_{-\alpha_{i}}-X_{\alpha_{j}}^{*}\wedge X^{*}_{-\alpha_{j}}\bigr),
\]
which identifies $V_{-}$. The computation on $V_{+}$ is identical.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{selfduality}
Let $G/K$ be a Hermitian symmetric space of complex dimension $n$. For $n\ge2$, a two-form is \emph{self-dual} (resp.\ \emph{anti-self-dual}) if it belongs in the sum of positive (resp.\ negative) eigenspaces of $*_{\Phi}$. Namely,
\[\Lambda^{2,+}{\mathfrak p}_\mathbb{C}^{*}=V_{+}\oplus\mathbb{C}\omega \qquad \text{ and }\qquad \Lambda^{2,-}{\mathfrak p}_\mathbb{C}^{*}=V_{-}.\] 
For $n=1$, we set $\Phi\coloneqq 0$ and declare every two-form to be self-dual.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{ex:selfdualsmall}
For $n=1$, the volume form coincides with $\omega$, $*_{\Phi}=0$, both eigenspaces are trivial and $\Lambda^{2}{\mathfrak p}_\mathbb{C}^{*}=\mathbb{C}\omega$. For $n=2$, $\Phi$ is
the $0$-form $1$, so $*_{\Phi}=*$ and the two positive eigenvalues coincide, recovering the classical $\Lambda^{2,\pm}$. For $n>2$ one has $\dim\Lambda^{2,+}=n^{2}-n+1<n^{2}-1=\dim\Lambda^{2,-}.$
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:proj}
Let $G/K$ be a Hermitian symmetric space of complex dimension $n$. For the self-dual elements fixed in \cref{selfdualelements}, the \emph{self-dual projection} is
\[\Pi^{+}:=\dfrac{\Lambda_{\omega}}{n}\,\omega
+\sum_{i<j}^{n}\bigl(\Lambda_{\eta_{ij}}\eta_{ij}+\Lambda_{\theta_{ij}}\theta_{ij}\bigr),\]
where $\Lambda_{\varphi}(\cdot)=(\varphi,\cdot)_{\lambda}$ denotes contraction.
For $n=2$, this is the classical $\Pi^{+}=(1+*)/2$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:cliffordomega}
The Clifford action of the Kähler form satisfies
${\gamma(\omega)}_{{|}_{\Lambda^{k}{\mathfrak p}_\mathbb{C}^{-\,*}}}=i(2k-n)\,\mathrm{id}$. In particular,
${\gamma(\omega)}_{{|}_{\Lambda^{2k}{\mathfrak p}_\mathbb{C}^{-\,*}}}=i(4k-n)\,\mathrm{id}$ for $0\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
\begin{align*}
\gamma(\omega)
&=\gamma\left(i\sum_{j=1}^n X_{\alpha_j}^*\wedge X_{-\alpha_j}^*\right)=
i
\sum_{j=1}^n(\gamma(X_{\alpha_j}^*)\gamma(X_{-\alpha_j}^*)+\mathrm{id})=i
\left(\sum_{j\in I}\mathrm{id}-\sum_{j\not\in I}\mathrm{id}\right)=i(2k-n)\mathrm{id}.
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{prop:norm}
Let $G/K$ be of complex dimension $n$ and let
$\zeta\in\Lambda^{2,+}(G/K,i\mathbb{R})$. Then,
\[\bigl|\gamma_{{|}_{S^{+}}}(\zeta)\bigr|^{2}=a_n|\zeta|^{2},\qquad \text{where} \qquad 
a_n=
\begin{cases}
2^{\,n-1}, & n\ne2,\\[2pt]
2^n, & n=2 .
\end{cases}
\]
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
We work in the orthonormal basis $\{\omega/\sqrt n,\eta_{ij},\theta_{ij}\}$. Since $\gamma(a)^{*}=-\gamma(a)$, \cref{lem:cliffordomega} gives
\[
\Bigl|\gamma_{{|}_{S^{+}}}\Bigl(\tfrac{\omega}{\sqrt n}\Bigr)\Bigr|^{2} =-\frac{1}{n}\ensuremath{\mathrm{tr}}\bigl(\gamma_{{|}_{S^{+}}}(\omega)^{2}\bigr)
=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{\substack{k=0\\ k\ \mathrm{even}}}^{n}(2k-n)^{2}\binom nk=\begin{cases}
    2^{n-1}, & n\ne 2
    \\
    2^n, &n=2.
\end{cases} 
\]
For the remaining basis elements,
$\gamma(\eta_{ij})^{2}=-1-\gamma(X^{*}_{2i-1})\gamma(X^{*}_{2j-1})\gamma(X^{*}_{2i})\gamma(X^{*}_{2j})$,
and for $n\ne2$ the second summand is off-diagonal, so
$|{\gamma}_{{|}_{S^{+}}}(\eta_{ij})|^{2}=\dim S^{+}=2^{n-1}$, and the same holds for $\theta_{ij}$. The claim for two-forms follows from orthogonality of \cref{selfdualelements} and this is carried for $i\mathbb{R}$-valued forms as
well. For $n=2$ each of the three basis elements contributes the factor $4$, as a
direct computation from \cref{eq:cliffordn2}.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:Qzero}
If $\dim(S^+\otimes E_\nu)=m=2^{n-1}$, then $\bigl(\mathcal{Q}_0(\psi)\psi,\psi\bigr)
=\frac{m-1}{m}\,|\psi|^{4}
=\bigl\langle\mathcal{Q}_0(\psi),\mathcal{Q}_0(\psi)\bigr\rangle.$
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Applying $\mathcal{Q}_0(\psi)=\psi\psi^*-\frac{1}{m}|\psi|^2\mathrm{id}$ to $\psi$ we get $\mathcal{Q}_0(\psi)\psi=\left(1-\frac{1}{m}\right)|\psi|^2\psi$. Thus $(\mathcal{Q}_0(\psi)\psi,\psi) =\frac{m-1}{m}|\psi|^4$. Also, $
\ensuremath{\mathrm{tr}}(\mathcal{Q}_0(\psi)^2)=\ensuremath{\mathrm{tr}}\left((\psi\psi^*)^2-\frac{2|\psi|^2}{m}\psi\psi^*+\frac{|\psi|^4}{m^2}\mathrm{id}\right)=|\psi|^4-\frac{2}{m}|\psi|^4+\frac{1}{m}|\psi|^4=\frac{m-1}{m}|\psi|^4.$
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{Qnot}
If $n\geq 4$ and $c$ is a constant, the condition $\mathcal{Q}_0(\psi)=ic \gamma(\omega)$ forces $\psi$ to be $0$.
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
The condition reads $\psi\psi^{*}\,=\,\frac{1}{m}|\psi|^{2}\,\mathrm{id}\,+\,c\,i\gamma(\omega)$. By \cref{lem:cliffordomega}, the right-hand side is diagonal for the decomposition of $S^{+}\otimes E_\nu$ by degree,                                           
with eigenvalue
\[\frac{1}{m}|\psi|^{2}-c(4k-n) \quad \text{ of multiplicity }\binom{n}{2k}\text{ on the k-th summand}.\] 
The numbers $4k-n$, $0\le k\le\lfloor
n/2\rfloor$, are pairwise distinct, so the map assigning $k$ to $\tfrac{1}{m}|\psi|^{2}-c(4k-n)$, $c\neq0$,
is injective and at most one of its values vanishes. The left-hand side has rank at most one, so at most one of these eigenvalues is non-zero. Hence
$\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1\le2$, that is, \ $n\le3$. For $n\ge4$, $c=0$ and
$|\psi|=0$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
\label{prop:topological}
Let $M=G/K$ be compact of complex dimension $n\ge2$, $E_{\nu}$ a one-dimensional
admissible twist and $A\in\mathcal{A}$. Then
\[
\int_{M}\Bigl(-\bigl|F^{+}_{A}\bigr|^{2}+\bigl|F^{-}_{A}\bigr|^{2}\Bigr){{\mathrm{vol}}}_{M}
+c\,\bigl\langle c_{1}(\mathcal{L}_{\nu})^{2}\smile[\omega]^{n-2},[M]\bigr\rangle
\ \ge\ \frac{(n-2)}{n\,{\mathrm{vol}}(M)}\biggl|\int_{M}\Lambda_{\omega}F_{A}\,{{\mathrm{vol}}}_{M}\biggr|^{2},
\]
where $c=4\pi^{2}/(n-2)!$, with equality, for $n>2$, if and only if
$\Lambda_{\omega}F_{A}$ is constant. For $n=2$, the formula is the classical topological identity and equality holds for every $A\in\mathcal{A}$.
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
By \cref{def:twistedhodge} and \cref{lib1},
$(*_{\Phi}F_{A},F_{A})_{\tau}\Omega=F_{A}\wedge\Phi\wedge\tau(F_{A})$, and since $\Phi$ is closed the integral of this expression is independent of $A$, hence a multiple of
$\langle c_{1}(\mathcal{L}_{\nu})^{2}\smile[\omega]^{n-2},[M]\rangle$, where $\mathcal{L}_{\nu}=\mathcal{E}_{\nu}\otimes \mathcal{E}_{\nu}$                  
. We write $F$ for $F_{A}$. Setting $F_{\omega}\coloneqq (\Lambda_{\omega}F)\omega/n$ and decomposing $\Pi^{+}F=F_{\omega}+F_{{|}_{V_+}}$, $F_{{|}_{V_-}}:=F-F_{\omega}-F_{{|}_{V_+}}$, \cref{prop:eigen} gives
\[
(*_{\Phi}F,F)_\tau=|F_{{|}_{V_+}}|^{2}-|F_{{|}_{V_-}}|^{2}+(n-1)|F_{\omega}|^{2}
=|F^{+}|^{2}-|F^{-}|^{2}+(n-2)|F_{\omega}|^{2}.
\]
Since $|F_{\omega}|^{2}=|\Lambda_{\omega}F|^{2}/n$, the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality
$\bigl|\int_{M}\Lambda_{\omega}F\ {\mathrm{vol}}_M\bigr|^{2}\le n{\mathrm{vol}}(M)\int_{M}|F_{\omega}|^{2}\ {\mathrm{vol}}_M$
holds, with equality if and only if $\Lambda_{\omega}F$ is constant. Rearranging the terms gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{theo:var}
Let $M=G/K$ be compact of complex dimension $n$, let $E_{\nu}$ be a one-dimensional admissible twist and let $A\in\mathcal{A}$. A pair $(\psi,A)\in \mathcal{C}_{SD}$ is an absolute minimum of the energy functional $\mathcal{E}_{{|}_{\mathcal{C}_{SD}}}$ if
\begin{equation}\label{swgen}
D_{A}^+\psi=0,
\qquad
F^{+}_{A}=-\frac{a_{n}}{8}\,\sigma(\psi)^{+},\qquad \Lambda_{\omega}F_{A}\text{ is constant.}
\end{equation}
 The last condition is vacuous for $n=2$, and is automatic for every $A\in\mathcal{A}^G$ by \cref{lem:Fomega}.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
We write $F$ for $F_{A}$. By the generalised Lichnerowicz formula in \cite{LM89} and the fact that on $\mathcal{C}_{SD}$ we have $F^-=0$, the first and third terms of \cref{eq:energy} combine into
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{E}(\psi,A)\coloneqq\int_{M}\left(
\bigl|D_{A}^+\psi\bigr|^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\gamma(F^{+})\psi,\psi\bigr)
+\bigl|\,F\,\bigr|^{2}
+\frac{a_{n}\bigl|\gamma(\sigma(\psi)^{+})\bigr|^{2}}{32}
\right){{\mathrm{vol}}}_{M}.
\end{equation}
We isolate the square of the Dirac operator and assume that $n> 2$. The remaining terms are 
\begin{equation}\label{presquare}
    -\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\gamma(F^{+})\psi,\psi\bigr)
+\frac{1}{2^{-n+6}}|\,\gamma(\sigma(\psi)^{+})\,|^{2}+|\,F\,|^{2}.
\end{equation}
By \cref{prop:norm}, $|\,\gamma(F^{+})\,|^{2}=2^{n-1}|\,F^{+}\,|^{2}$, and by the definition of $\sigma$ in \cref{eq:sigma},
\[\bigl(\gamma(F^{+})\psi,\psi\bigr)=-\bigl\langle\gamma(F^{+}),\gamma(\sigma(\psi)^{+})\bigr\rangle.\] Completing the square in \cref{presquare}, we get
\[
2^{\,n-6}\Bigl(2^{-n+4}\gamma(F^{+})+\gamma(\sigma(\psi)^{+})\Bigr)^{2}
\  -|\,F^{+}\,|^{2}+|\,F^{-}\,|^{2}.
\]
So, 
\begin{equation}\label{squares}
\mathcal{E}(\psi,A)=
\bigl\|D_{A}\psi\bigr\|_{L^2}^{2}
+2^{n-6}\bigl\|2^{-n+4} \, \gamma(F^+)+\gamma(\sigma(\psi)^+)\bigr\|_{L^2}^{2}+\int_M( -|\,F^{+}\,|^{2}+|\,F^{-}\,|^{2}){\mathrm{vol}}_M ,
\end{equation}
and the last term is bounded below by \cref{prop:topological}, with equality exactly when $\Lambda_{\omega}F$ is constant. For $n=1$, $\psi$ and $F$ are zero, and the claim follows. For $n=2$, $|\,\gamma(F^{+})\,|^{2}=4|\,F^{+}\,|^{2}$, and the square completes to $F^+=-1/2\sigma(\psi)^+$. The last summand is purely topological and the constancy condition is empty, which is the classical situation.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:equivmin}
Let $M=G/K$ be compact. Every pair $(\psi,A)$ with $A\in\mathcal{A}^G$ satisfying
\cref{swgen} is an absolute minimum of $\mathcal{E}_{{|}_{\mathcal{C}_{SD}}}$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{eqSW}
    The $it\omega$-perturbed equations of \cref{swgen} are the \emph{equivariant Seiberg--Witten equations}. 
    \begin{equation}\label{swcngen}
D_{A}^+\psi=0,
\qquad
F^{+}_{A}+it\omega=-\frac{a_{n}}{8}\,\sigma(\psi)^{+}.
\end{equation}
   We denote by $\mathcal{S}_\nu^\infty$ the space of their solutions.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{theo:monopole}
Let $(G/K,\lambda B_{{\mathfrak p}})$ be of complex dimension $n$, $E_{\nu}$ be a one-dimensional admissible twist and $A\in\mathcal{A}^G$. With $c_{n}(t,\nu,\lambda)=8n\bigl(t+\tfrac{\nu}{2\lambda}\bigr)$, the $it\omega$-perturbed monopole equation of \cref{swgen} is equivalent to the
pointwise system
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}(n-4k)\bigl|\psi^{(2k)}(g)\bigr|^{2}=c_{n}(t,\nu,\lambda),
\qquad
\bigl(\gamma(\eta_{ij})\psi,\psi\bigr)(g)=\bigl(\gamma(\theta_{ij})\psi,\psi\bigr)(g)=0,
\quad 1\le i<j\le n .
\end{equation*}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
The perturbed $it\omega$-monopole reads $2F_{A_{E_{\nu}}}^{+}+it\omega=-\tfrac{a_n}{8}\sigma(\psi)^{+}$, since \cref{linebndleequiv} indicates that $F_{A}=2F_{A_{E_{\nu}}}$. By \cref{lem:Fomega}, the left-hand side is $\bigl(\tfrac{\nu i}{2\lambda}+it\bigr)\omega$, so all $\eta_{ij}$- and $\theta_{ij}$-components of the left-hand side vanish, which leads to the second and third families of equations. Contracting with $\omega$, the left-hand side contributes $n\bigl(\tfrac{\nu i}{2\lambda}+it\bigr)$, while the right-hand side, by
\cref{eq:sigma} and \cref{lem:cliffordomega}, contributes
\[
-\frac{a_n}{8}\cdot\frac{1}{a_n}\bigl(\gamma(\omega)\psi,\psi\bigr)
=-\frac18\sum_{k}i(4k-n)\bigl|\psi^{(2k)}\bigr|^{2}.
\]
Multiplying by $8/i$ gives the first equation.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
\label{ex:lowdimmono}
Writing $\psi_{1},\dots,\psi_{2^{n-1}}$ for the components in the basis of \cref{uweights}, ordered by increasing degree, \cref{theo:monopole} reads:
\[
\begin{array}{ccccc}
n
& &
\omega\text{-condition}
& &
\eta_{ij}\ \&\ \theta_{ij}\text{-condition}
\\[2pt]
\hline
\\
2 & &
{2|\psi_{1}|^{2}-2|\psi_{2}|^{2}=c_{2}} & &
{\psi_{1}\overline{\psi_{2}}=0}
\\[10pt]
3 & &
{3|\psi_{1}|^{2}-|\psi_{2}|^{2}-|\psi_{3}|^{2}-|\psi_{4}|^{2}=c_{3}}
& &
{\psi_{1}\overline{\psi_{2}}}
={\psi_{1}\overline{\psi_{3}}}
={\psi_{1}\overline{\psi_{4}}=0}
\\[10pt]
4 & &
{4|\psi_{1}|^{2}-4|\psi_{8}|^{2}=c_{4}} & &
{\psi_{1}\overline{\psi_{2}}+\overline{\psi_{7}}\psi_{8}}=0,
\quad 
{\psi_{1}\overline{\psi_{3}}-\overline{\psi_{6}}\psi_{8}}=0,
\\
& & & &{\psi_{1}\overline{\psi_{4}}+\overline{\psi_{5}}\psi_{8}}=0,\quad
{\psi_{1}\overline{\psi_{7}}+\overline{\psi_{2}}\psi_{8}}=0,
\\
& & & &\psi_{1}\overline{\psi_{6}}-\overline{\psi_{3}}\psi_{8}=0,\quad
\psi_{1}\overline{\psi_{5}}+\overline{\psi_{4}}\psi_{8}=0.
\end{array}
\]
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- proposition-16: body_md -->
\label{monoshape}
The equations of \cref{theo:monopole} take the form
\[
\sum_{k}d_{k}\bigl|\psi^{(2k)}\bigr|^{2}=c_{n}(t,\nu,\lambda),
\qquad
\sum_{i_{1}\neq i_{2}}\varepsilon_{i_{1}i_{2}}\,\psi_{i_{1}}\overline{\psi_{i_{2}}}=0,
\qquad d_{k}\in\mathbb{Z},\ \varepsilon_{i_{1}i_{2}}\in\{0,\pm1\}.
\]
<!-- end proposition-16 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
We refer to \cite{Tsi26} for the proof.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- proposition-17: body_md -->
\label{prop:gaugeeq}
A gauge transformation $u$ preserves the set of pairs $(\psi,A)$ for which
$A\in\mathcal{A}^G$ if and only if $u\colon G/K\to U(1)$ is constant.
Consequently, the equivariant gauge group is $\mathcal{G}_{eq}\simeq U(1)$.
<!-- end proposition-17 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Under a gauge transformation $u:G/K\to\ensuremath{\mathrm{U}}(1)$, the connection changes by the Maurer-Cartan term $-2u^{-1}du$. For $(u\psi,(u^{-1})^*A)$ to remain an equivariant solution, $u^{-1}du$ must be a $G$-invariant $1$-form. Since the action of $K$ on ${\mathfrak p}$ is irreducible, it has no non-zero trivial subrepresentation, therefore $u^{-1}du=0$. So, $du=0$, and since $G/K$ is connected, $u$ is constant. The converse is readily verified.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{def:eqsolutions}
We denote $\mathcal{M_\nu^\infty}(c_n)$ the moduli space $\mathcal{S}_{\nu}^{\infty}(c_n)/\mathcal{G}$. The sets of \emph{equivariant solutions} are
\[
\mathcal{S}_{\nu,eq}^{\infty}(c_n):=\bigl\{(\psi,A)\ \text{satisfying \cref{swcngen}}\, |\, A\in\mathcal{A}^G\bigr\},
\qquad
\mathcal{S}_{\nu,eq}^{L^{2}}(c_n)\coloneqq\mathcal{S}^{\infty}_{\nu,eq}(c_n)\cap\bigl\{\psi\in\ker_{L^{2}}D^{+}_{0}\bigr\}.
\]
The corresponding moduli sets are
$\mathcal{M}^{\infty}_{\nu,eq}(c_n)\coloneqq\mathcal{S}^{\infty}_{\nu,eq}(c_n)/\mathcal{G}_{eq}$ and
$\mathcal{M}^{L^{2}}_{\nu,eq}(c_n)\coloneqq\mathcal{S}^{L^{2}}_{\nu,eq}(c_n)/\mathcal{G}_{eq}$.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- proposition-18: body_md -->
\label{cor:muzero}
    Let $G/K$ be a compact irreducible Hermitian symmetric space, let $E_{\mu\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}}$ be a one-dimensional $K$-representation and let $\psi\in H^{(0,0)}(G/K,E_{\mu\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}})$ have non-zero constant pointwise norm. Then $\mu=0$.
<!-- end proposition-18 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Indeed, $\psi$ is then nowhere vanishing and holomorphic, hence trivialises $\mathcal{E}_\mu$ as a holomorphic line bundle, thus $c_1(\mathcal{E}_\mu) = 0$. By \cref{lem:Fomega}, 
\[F_{A_{E\mu}} = \frac{\mu i}{4\lambda}\omega.\] 
Since $[\omega]\neq 0$, this forces $\mu= 0$.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{uniquew}
    The Weyl group acts simply transitively on the Weyl chambers of the regular elements. Since $\langle\rho_{{\mathfrak g}},\check\alpha_{i}\rangle=1$ for every simple root $\alpha_{i}$, $\langle w(\mu+\rho_{{\mathfrak k}}),\check\alpha_{i}\rangle\ge1>0$, where $\langle\lambda,\check{\alpha}\rangle
 =2(\lambda,\alpha)/(\alpha,\alpha)$. So, $w(\mu+\rho_{{\mathfrak k}})$ is regular dominant and, by transitivity, a regular Weyl orbit meets the open dominant chamber once.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{rhoND}
        If $G/K$ is an irreducible Hermitian symmetric space and ${\alpha\in \Delta_{{\mathfrak p}}^+}$, then ${( \rho_{{\mathfrak p}},\alpha )=N}$ if G/K is of Type C\textsubscript{I} and ${( \rho_{{\mathfrak p}},\alpha)=N/2}$ otherwise.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
By \cref{Z_0*rho}, $\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}$ is proportional to $Z_0^{*}$, and the ordering of Convention \ref{conventionHSS} gives $\alpha(Z_{0})=i$ for every $\alpha\in\Delta_{\mathfrak p}^{+}$, so $(\rho_{{\mathfrak p}},\alpha)$ is independent of $\alpha$. Its value is read off type by type.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- convention-1: body_md -->
\label{conv:weyl}
We set ${s_{i}\coloneqq s_{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_i-\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_{i+1}}}$, ${\tilde{s}_{i}\coloneqq s_{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_i+\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_{i+1}}}$ and ${\check{s}_{p,i} \coloneqq s_{p-1} }$ when $i$ even and ${\check{s}_{p,i} \coloneqq \tilde{s}_{p-1}} $ when ${i}$ odd. Products of reflections are composed left to right, that is, $s_{i}s_{j}$ means that \emph{we first apply $s_{i}$, then $s_{j}$}.
<!-- end convention-1 -->
<!-- proposition-19: body_md -->
\label{weylelem}
    Let ${G/K}$ be a non-exceptional, compact, irreducible Hermitian symmetric space of complex dimension ${n}$. The unique Weyl group element ${w\in W_G}$ such that ${\lambda_\nu\coloneqq w(\nu\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}+\rho_{\mathfrak k})-\rho_{\mathfrak g}}$ is dominant for G when $\nu\geq 1$ is ${w= {id}}$. For $-1< \nu <1 $ there is no such element. For $\nu\leq -1$, ${w}$ is given explicitly in the following table and satisfies ${\ell(w)=n}$.
    
\vspace{2mm}
    \begin{center}
    \small
\renewcommand{1.3}{1.3}
\begin{NiceTabular}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}[hlines]
\textbf{Type} & \textbf{G} & ${W_G}$ & ${w}$  \\ 
\hline 
A\textsubscript{III} (${ p\geq q} $) & $ {\ensuremath{\mathrm{SU}}(p+q)} $
& ${\langle s_{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_i-\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_j}\rangle}$ & ${\prod\limits_{j=1}^{q}s_{p+j-1}\cdot s_{p+j-2} \cdots s_{j}}$\\ 
BD\textsubscript{I} ($ {p> 2 }$, odd) & $ {\ensuremath{\mathrm{SO}}(2+p)} $ & ${\langle s_{i}, s_{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_{\lceil p/2 \rceil}}\rangle}$ & ${\prod\limits_{i=1}^{\lfloor p/2 \rfloor}  s_i \cdot s_{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_{\lceil p/2\rceil}} \cdot \prod\limits_{i=1}^{\lfloor p/2\rfloor}  s_{\lfloor p/2\rfloor-i+1}}$ \\ 
BD\textsubscript{I} (${ p> 2} $, even) & $ {\ensuremath{\mathrm{SO}}(2+p) }$ & ${\langle s_{i}, \tilde{s}_{p/2}\rangle}$ &  ${\prod\limits_{i=1}^{p/2-1}  s_i \cdot \tilde{s}_{p/2} \cdot \prod\limits_{i=1}^{p/2}  s_{p/2+1-i}}$ \\ 
D\textsubscript{III}             
& $ {\ensuremath{\mathrm{SO}}(2p)} $& ${\langle s_{i},\tilde{s}_{p-1}\rangle}$ & ${\prod\limits_{i=1}^{ p-1}s_{p-i}\cdot s_{p-i+1}\cdot \cdots \cdot s_{p-2}\cdot\check{s}_{p,i}} $  \\ 
                                                                                                                                                                                       
C\textsubscript{I}  & $ {\ensuremath{\mathrm{Sp}}(p)}  $ & ${\langle s_{i}, s_{2\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_p}\rangle}$ & ${s_{2\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_p} (s_{p-1} s_{2\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_p}) \cdots  (s_1 \cdots  s_{p-1} s_{2\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_p})}$ \\ 
                                                             
                                                                                      
\end{NiceTabular}
\end{center}
<!-- end proposition-19 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
We proceed by finding an element for which the proposition holds and use Remark \ref{uniquew} to establish its uniqueness. From Lemma \ref{rhoND}, when $\nu\geq 1$ the dominance of $\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}$ implies that $(\nu-1)\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}$ is also dominant and therefore ${w=  {id}}$. For ${-1<\nu<1}$, suppose that there exists ${w\in W_G}$ such that ${\lambda_\nu}$ is dominant. The Weyl group preserves the invariant inner product and ${\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}\perp \Delta_{\mathfrak k}}$ by Lemma \ref{Z_0*rho},
\[{\|\lambda_\nu+\rho_{{\mathfrak g}}\|^2=\|w(\nu\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}+\rho_{{\mathfrak k}})\|^2=\|\nu\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}+\rho_{{\mathfrak k}}\|^2=\nu^2\|\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}\|^2+\|\rho_{{\mathfrak k}}\|^2<\|\rho_{{\mathfrak g}}\|^2.
}\]
But, ${\lambda_\nu}$ is dominant and therefore
\[{
\|\lambda_\nu+\rho_{{\mathfrak g}}\|^2
=
\|\rho_{{\mathfrak g}}\|^2
+2\langle\lambda_\nu,\rho_{{\mathfrak g}}\rangle
+\|\lambda_\nu\|^2
\geq
\|\rho_{{\mathfrak g}}\|^2.
}\]
Hence there is no ${w\in W_G}$ for which ${\lambda_\nu}$ is dominant when ${-1<\nu<1}$. For ${\nu\leq -1}$, we prove here the case of type A\textsubscript{III}. For the other cases we refer to \cite{Tsi26}.
        \[{\nu\rho_{\mathfrak p}+\rho_{{\mathfrak k}}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\underset{\eqqcolon A_i}{\underbrace{\tfrac{\nu q+p+1-2i}{2}}}\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_i+\sum_{j=1}^{q}\underset{\eqqcolon B_j}{\underbrace{\tfrac{-\nu p+q+1-2j}{2}}\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_{p+j}}.}\]
        We note that for ${1\leq i\leq p-1}$, ${A_i-A_{i+1}=1}$, and for all ${1\leq j\leq q-1}$, ${B_j-B_{j+1}=1}$.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                 
        For $\nu\leq -1$,  
        \[{B_q-A_1=\tfrac{-\nu p-q+1}{2}-\tfrac{\nu q+p-1}{2}=1-\tfrac{(\nu+1)(p+q)}{2}\geq 1.}\]
        In order for $\nu\rho_{\mathfrak p}+\rho_{{\mathfrak k}}$ to be dominant for ${\mathfrak g}$, even before subtracting $\rho_{\mathfrak g}$, we need to find an element ${w}$ such that 
        \[{w(\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_i)=\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_{q+i}, \quad 1\leq i\leq p, \quad  w(\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_{p+j})=\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_{j}, \quad 1\leq j\leq q.}\]
        So,
        \begin{align*}
            {w(\nu\rho_{\mathfrak p}+\rho_{{\mathfrak k}})-\rho_{\mathfrak g}}&{=\sum_{j=1}^{q}\tfrac{-\nu p+q+1-2j}{2}\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_j+\sum_{i=1}^{p}\tfrac{\nu q+p+1-2i}{2}\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_{q+i}-\sum_{j=1}^{p+q}\tfrac{p+q+1-2j}{2} \ensuremath{\varepsilon}_j}\\
            &{=\sum_{j=1}^{q}\tfrac{(-\nu-1)p }{2}\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_j+\sum_{i=1}^{p}\tfrac{(\nu+1)q }{2}\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_{q+i}}{=(-\nu-1)\tfrac{(p+q)}{2}\varpi_q,}
        \end{align*}   
        which is dominant for ${\mathfrak g}$. This unique Weyl group element is expressed in terms of ${s_{i}}$ as $w=\prod\limits_{j=1}^{q}s_{p+j-1}s_{p+j-2}\cdots s_{j}$ and therefore ${\ell(w)=pq}$.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{weylhwdim}
    Let ${G/K}$ be a compact, non-exceptional irreducible Hermitian symmetric space. The highest weight $\lambda_\nu$ of \cref{weylelem} as well as the dimension of ${\ker D(\mathcal{E}_\nu)}$ are given below.
    \vspace{2mm}
\LARGE
\newcommand{\rule[-4ex]{0pt}{8ex}}{\rule[-4ex]{0pt}{8ex}}
\newcommand{\rule[-8ex]{0pt}{19ex}}{\rule[-8ex]{0pt}{19ex}}
\begin{center}
\renewcommand{1.3}{1.6}
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{12pt}
\resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{ 
\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c@{\hspace{1.5em}}|}
\hline
\textbf{Type} & \textbf{G} & \textbf{$\lambda_\nu$} & \textbf{$\dim(\ker D(\mathcal{E}_\nu))$}\\
\hline
A\textsubscript{III} $(p\geq q)$ & $\ensuremath{\mathrm{SU}}(p+q)$ &
$\left\{\begin{array}{@{}l@{\hspace{1.5em}}l@{\hspace{1em}}}
(\nu-1)\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}, & \nu\geq 1\\[2ex]
-\tfrac{(\nu+1)(p+q)}{2}\varpi_{q}, & \nu\leq -1
\end{array}\right.$ &
$\rule[-8ex]{0pt}{19ex}\left\{\begin{array}{@{}l@{\hspace{1.5em}}l@{\hspace{1em}}}
\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{p}\prod_{j=p+1}^{p+q}\Bigl(1+\tfrac{(\nu-1)(p+q)}{2(j-i)}\Bigr), & \nu\geq 1\\[5ex]
\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{q}\prod_{j=q+1}^{p+q}\Bigl(1+\tfrac{(|\nu\,|-1)(p+q)}{2(j-i)}\Bigr), & \nu\leq -1
\end{array}\right.$\\
\hline
BD\textsubscript{I} $(p>2)$ & $\ensuremath{\mathrm{SO}}(2+p)$ & $(|\nu\,|-1)\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}$ &
$\rule[-4ex]{0pt}{8ex}|\nu\,|\,\dbinom{p-1+\tfrac{(|\nu\,|-1)p}{2}}{\tfrac{(|\nu\,|-1)p}{2}}$\\
\hline
D\textsubscript{III}, $p$ odd & $\ensuremath{\mathrm{SO}}(2p)$ &
$\left\{\begin{array}{@{}l@{\hspace{1.5em}}l@{\hspace{1em}}}
(\nu-1)\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}, & \nu\geq 1\\[2ex]
(|\nu\,|-1)(p-1)\varpi_{p-1}, & \nu\leq -1
\end{array}\right.$ &
$\rule[-8ex]{0pt}{19ex}\left\{\begin{array}{@{}l@{\hspace{1.5em}}l@{\hspace{1em}}}
\displaystyle\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq p}\Bigl(1+\tfrac{(\nu-1)(p-1)}{2p-(i+j)}\Bigr), & \nu\geq 1\\[5ex]
\dbinom{|\nu\,|(p-1)}{(|\nu\,|-1)(p-1)}\displaystyle\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq p-1}\Bigl(1+\tfrac{(|\nu\,|-1)(p-1)}{2p-(i+j)}\Bigr), & \nu\leq -1
\end{array}\right.$\\
\hline
D\textsubscript{III}, $p$ even & $\ensuremath{\mathrm{SO}}(2p)$ & $(|\nu\,|-1)\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}$ &
$\rule[-4ex]{0pt}{8ex}\displaystyle\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq p}\Bigl(1+\tfrac{(|\nu\,|-1)(p-1)}{2p-(i+j)}\Bigr)$\\
\hline
C\textsubscript{I} & $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Sp}}(p)$ & $(|\nu\,|-1)\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}$ &
$\rule[-4ex]{0pt}{8ex}\displaystyle\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq p}\Bigl(1+\tfrac{(|\nu\,|-1)(p+1)}{2p+2-(i+j)}\Bigr)\dbinom{p+\frac{(|\nu\,|-1)(p+1)}{2}}{\frac{(|\nu\,|-1)(p+1)}{2}}$\\
\hline
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           
\end{tabular}}
\vspace{1mm}
\end{center}
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
The proof is a combination of \cref{weylelem} and the Weyl dimension formula. We refer to \cite{Tsi26} for more details.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- example-4: body_md -->
\label{ex:su3realisation}
For ${\mathfrak g}=\mathfrak{su}(3)$, type A\textsubscript{III}, $p=2$, $q=1$, $n=2$, $N=3$, admissible twists
are $\nu=1+2\kappa/3$, $\kappa\in\mathbb{Z}$. With $\varpi_{1}=\tfrac23\epsilon_{1}-\tfrac13\epsilon_{2}-\tfrac13\epsilon_{3}$
and $\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}=\tfrac32\varpi_{2}$,
\[
\ker D^{+}(\mathcal{E}_{\nu})=
\begin{cases}
V_{3(\nu-1)\varpi_{2}/2}, & \nu\ge1,\\
0, & \nu=\pm\tfrac13,\\
V_{-3(\nu+1)\varpi_{1}/2}, & \nu\le-1,
\end{cases}
\qquad \dim(\ker D^{+}(E_{\nu}))=\frac{9\nu^{2}-1}{8}.
\]
<!-- end example-4 -->
<!-- proposition-20: body_md -->
\label{exeptweylelem}
    Let ${G/K}$ be an exceptional, compact, irreducible Hermitian symmetric space of complex dimension ${n}$. The unique Weyl group element ${w\in W_G}$ such that ${\lambda_\nu\coloneqq w(\nu\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}+\rho_{\mathfrak k})-\rho_{\mathfrak g}}$ is dominant for G when $\nu\geq 1$ is ${w= {id}}$. For $-1< \nu <1 $ there is no such element. For $\nu\leq -1$, ${w}$ is given explicitly in the following table and satisfies ${\ell(w)=n}$. Here ${s_i\coloneqq s_{\alpha_i}}$.
    \vspace{2mm}
    \begin{center}
\renewcommand{1.3}{1.3}
\small
\begin{NiceTabular}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}[hlines]
\textbf{Type} & \textbf{G} & ${w}$ \\ 
\hline
E\textsubscript{III} &  $ {E_{6}       
}$ & ${s_6\cdot s_5\cdot s_4\cdot s_2\cdot s_3\cdot s_1\cdot s_4\cdot s_3\cdot s_5\cdot s_4\cdot s_2\cdot s_6\cdot s_5\cdot s_4\cdot s_3\cdot s_1 }$ \\ 
E\textsubscript{VII} & $ {E_{7}        
}$ & ${s_7\cdot s_6\cdot s_5\cdot s_4\cdot s_2\cdot s_3\cdot s_1\cdot s_4\cdot s_3\cdot s_5\cdot s_4\cdot s_2\cdot s_6\cdot s_5\cdot s_4\cdot s_3\cdot s_1\cdot s_7\cdot s_6\cdot s_5\cdot s_4\cdot s_2\cdot s_3\cdot s_4\cdot s_5\cdot s_6\cdot s_7 } $
\end{NiceTabular}
\end{center}
\vspace{2mm}
<!-- end proposition-20 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
For $\nu\ge1$ and $-1<\nu<1$ the argument of \cref{weylelem} applies
verbatim. For E\textsubscript{III} with $\nu\le-1$ one has
$\nu\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}+\rho_{{\mathfrak k}}=\varpi_{1}+\dots+\varpi_{5}+(6\nu-5)\varpi_{6}$, and the
element above satisfies $w(\varpi_{6})=-\varpi_{1}$ and
$w(\rho_{{\mathfrak k}})=-5\varpi_{1}+\varpi_{2}+\dots+\varpi_{6}$, thus $w(\nu\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}+\rho_{{\mathfrak k}})-\rho_{{\mathfrak g}}=6(-\nu-1)\varpi_{1}$, dominant. For E\textsubscript{VII} we refer to \cite{Tsi26}.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{weylhwdim2}
    The highest weight $\lambda_\nu$ of \cref{exeptweylelem} for the exceptional irreducible Hermitian symmetric spaces of type E\textsubscript{III} is $(\nu-1)\rho_{\mathfrak p}$ for $\nu\geq 1$ and $6(|\nu\,|-1)\varpi_{1}$ for $\nu \leq -1$. For type E\textsubscript{VII}, it is $(|\nu\,|-1)\rho_{\mathfrak p}$ for all admissible $\nu$.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{coro:neven}
     Let ${G/K}$ be a compact Hermitian symmetric space of complex dimension $n$ and let
    ${\lambda_\nu=w(\nu\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}+\rho_{\mathfrak k})-\rho_{\mathfrak g}}$ be the highest weight of Propositions \ref{weylelem} and \ref{exeptweylelem}. For $\nu\leq-1$, ${\ell(w)=n}$ and, consequently,
    \[
        {\ker D^+(\mathcal{E}_{\nu})\neq0
        \iff n\in2\mathbb{Z}, \qquad\ker D^-(\mathcal{E}_{\nu})\neq0
        \iff n\in2\mathbb{Z}+1}.
    \]
                                                                 
     For $\nu\geq1$, the Weyl element is $w=\mathrm{id}$, so the representation occurs in $\ker D^+(\mathcal{E}_{\nu})$ and not in $\ker D^-(\mathcal{E}_{\nu})$. For $|\nu|<1$, the kernel in question vanishes.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
The proof is a direct consequence of \cref{weylelem}, \cref{exeptweylelem} and Landweber's condition mentioned above.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{coro:nevennc}
        Let G/K be a non-compact, irreducible 2$n$-dimensional Hermitian symmetric space, ${E_{\nu\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}}}$ a one-dimensional admissible twist and ${\delta_\nu\coloneqq\nu\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}+\rho_{\mathfrak k}}$. If $\nu\geq 1$, 
        \begin{align*}
            {\ker_{L^2} \, D^+(\mathcal{E}_{\nu\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}})} \text{ is a discrete series representation} & {\iff  n\in 2\mathbb{Z}.}\\
            {\ker_{L^2} \, D^-(\mathcal{E}_{\nu\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}})} \text{ is a discrete series representation} & {\iff  n\in 2\mathbb{Z}+1.}
        \end{align*}
        In either parity, the non-zero half-spinor kernel has Harish-Chandra parameter $\delta_\nu$. If $\nu\leq -1$, the realisation is in the positive half-spinor kernel, with the same parameter. If $|\nu\,|<1$ the kernel in question vanishes.
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{Mmatrix}
    $\mathcal{Q}(\psi)$ is Hermitian, positive semi-definite, of rank at most one.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
Given that ${\mathcal{Q}(\psi)=\psi\psi^*}$, it is self-adjoint. It is positive semi-definite since for ${v\in \mathbb{C}^{2^{n-1}}}$, $v^*\psi\psi^*v$$=(\psi^* v)^*\psi^*v=|\psi^* v|^2\geq 0$. Moreover, each column is a multiple of $\psi$, thus its rank is at most one.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
Let $m^+=2^{n-1}$. The following set is called the \emph{Veronese cone}
    \[{\mathcal{V}\coloneqq\{A \in \ensuremath{\mathrm{Herm}\,}(m^+) \, | \, A \text{ positive semi-definite}, \, \text{rk} A\leq 1\}}.\]
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- example-5: body_md -->
According to \cref{ex:lowdimmono} for ${n=3}$, ${\pi:\ensuremath{\mathrm{Herm}\,}(4)\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}\oplus\mathbb{C}^{3}}$ and $v_3$ are
        \[{\pi(M)=(3M_{11}-M_{22}-M_{33}-M_{44},M_{12},M_{13}, M_{14}), \qquad v_3=(c_3,0,0,0)}\]
<!-- end example-5 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
From \cref{eqSW} and \cref{theo:monopole}, $\mathcal{S}_{\nu}^\infty(c_{n})$ denotes the space of smooth solutions. Let
\[{\mathcal{Z}_{\nu,eq}^\infty(c_{n})\coloneqq \left\{\psi\in\ker D^+ \,|\,\mathcal{Q}_g(\psi)\in \mathcal{X}_n(c_{n})\text{ for every }g\in G\right\}.}\]
It is immediate from \cref{eq:Lambdavanish} that ${\mathcal{S}_{\nu,eq}^\infty(c_{n})\simeq\mathcal{Z}_{\nu,eq}^\infty(c_{n})\times \{pt\}}$, where ${\{pt\}=\{\Lambda_{E_\nu}\}}$. Consequently,
\[
{\mathcal{M}_{\nu,eq}^\infty(c_{n})\simeq
\mathcal{Z}_{\nu,eq}^\infty(c_{n})/\mathcal{G}_{eq}.}
\]
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- proposition-21: body_md -->
\label{hodgeserre}
Let $M$ be a compact complex manifold of dimension ${n}$ and $\mathcal{E}$ be a Hermitian holomorphic vector bundle over $M$. 
\[{H^{(0,q)}\,(M,\mathcal{E})\simeq H^{(0,n-q)}\,(M,\mathcal{K}\otimes \mathcal{E}^*)^*.}\]
<!-- end proposition-21 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{nu2nu}
    For a compact irreducible Hermitian symmetric space of even complex dimension, 
\begin{equation*}
    {\ker D^+ (\mathcal{E}_\nu)\, \simeq\, \ker D^+(\mathcal{E}_{-\nu})^*.}
\end{equation*}
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
From Theorems 3 and 4 of \cite{La00}, Theorem IV of \cite{Bo57} and Hodge--Serre duality we get
\[\ker D^{+}(\mathcal{E}_{\nu})=\bigoplus_{q\ \mathrm{even}}H^{(0,q)}\bigl(G/K,\mathcal{E}_{(\nu-1)}\bigr)\simeq \bigoplus_{q\ \mathrm{even}}H^{(0,n-q)}\bigl(G/K,\mathcal{E}_{(-\nu-1)}\bigr)^*=\ker D^{+}(\mathcal{E}_{-\nu})^*.\]
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
If ${u_I=X_{-\alpha_{i_1}}^*\wedge \cdots \wedge X_{-\alpha_{i_{2k}}}^*}$, ${I=\{ 1\leq i_1<\cdots<i_{2k}\leq n\}}$ is an element of ${S^+=\Lambda^{ev}{{\mathfrak p}_\mathbb{C}^-}^*}$, we denote by ${I^c}$ the complement of ${I}$. For $\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_I\in\{\pm1\}$ the \emph{complementary operator} $L$ satisfies
\[{L\, (a_Iu_I)\coloneqq \ensuremath{\varepsilon}_I\overline{a_I} u_{I^c}, \quad \text{ where }\quad  u_I\wedge u_{I^c}=\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_I\, u_{top}.}\]
Its extension on $S^+\otimes E_\nu$ by tensoring with $h^\#$ is denoted by the same symbol.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{Cmap}
 
 When $n$ is even, the operator ${L}$ is an antiunitary involution on ${S^+\otimes E_\nu}$ and satisfies
\begin{align*}
    {L\circ \epsilon\bigl(X_{-\alpha_i}^*\bigr)\circ \epsilon\bigl(X_{-\alpha_j}^*\bigr)}\,&={-\iota\bigl(X_{\alpha_i}^*\bigr)\circ \iota\bigl(X_{\alpha_j}^*\bigr)\circ L,}\\
    {L\circ \iota\bigl(X_{\alpha_i}^*\bigr)\circ \iota\bigl(X_{\alpha_j}^*\bigr)}\,&={-\epsilon\bigl(X_{-\alpha_i}^*\bigr)\circ \epsilon\bigl(X_{-\alpha_j}^*\bigr)\circ L.}
\end{align*}
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Immediate by applying the definitions.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- proposition-22: body_md -->
\label{XX}
Let ${n}$ be even. If ${\psi}$ satisfies the monopole conditions with parameter ${c_{n}}$, then ${L\psi}$ satisfies the same system with parameter ${-c_{n}}$.
<!-- end proposition-22 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
By \cref{selfduality} and Clifford multiplication $\gamma$ in \cref{sec:spin}, we note that
\begin{align}\label{geeii}
    \begin{split}
    {\gamma\bigl(\sqrt{2}\eta_{ij}\bigr)}\,&={2\left(\epsilon\bigl(X_{-\alpha_i}^*\bigr)\circ\epsilon\bigl(X_{-\alpha_j}^*\bigr)+\iota\bigl(X_{\alpha_i}^*\bigr)\circ\iota\bigl(X_{\alpha_j}^*\bigr)\right)}\\
    {\gamma\bigl(\sqrt{2}\theta_{ij}\bigr)}\,&={2i\left(\epsilon\bigl(X_{-\alpha_i}^*\bigr)\circ\epsilon\bigl(X_{-\alpha_j}^*\bigr)-\iota\bigl(X_{\alpha_i}^*\bigr)\circ\iota\bigl(X_{\alpha_j}^*\bigr)\right)}
    \end{split}
\end{align}
According to \cref{Cmap}, ${L}$ anti-commutes with both ${\gamma\left(\sqrt{2}\eta_{ij}\right)}$ and ${\gamma\left(\sqrt{2}\theta_{ij}\right)}$. Since ${L}$ is also unitary, the second and third families of equations are preserved by ${L}$ due to the following properties.
\[{\bigl(\gamma(\sqrt{2}\eta_{ij}) L\psi,L\psi\bigr)= -\tau(\gamma(\sqrt{2}\eta_{ij})\psi,\psi)
,\qquad \bigl(\gamma(\sqrt{2}\theta_{ij})L\psi,L\psi\bigr)=-\tau\bigl(\gamma(\sqrt{2}\theta_{ij})\psi,\psi\bigr).
}\]
Additionally, ${L}$ maps the component of degree ${2k}$ to that of degree ${n-2k}$. Therefore, the corresponding coefficient in the first equation of the monopole conditions becomes ${n-4\left(n/2-k\right)=-(n-4k)}.$ Consequently, $\sum_{k}(n-4k)|(L\psi)^{(2k)}|^{2}=-\sum_{k}(n-4k)|\psi^{(2k)}|^{2}$.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{theo:parity}
Let ${(G/K,\lambda{B_{{\mathfrak g}}}_{|_{{\mathfrak p}}}})$ be a $2n$-dimensional irreducible compact Hermitian symmetric space, $ {E_\nu}$ be a one-dimensional admissible twist and $ {A\in \mathcal{A}^G}$. For ${n}$ odd the moduli are asymmetric in ${c_{n}\lessgtr0}$, while for ${n}$ even the symmetry leads to 
\[{\mathcal{M}_{\nu,eq}^\infty(c_{n})\simeq\mathcal{M}_{-\nu,eq}^\infty(-c_{n})}.\] 
The reducible wall is always at ${c_{n}=0}$, that is, ${t=-\tfrac{\nu}{2\lambda}}$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
The asymmetry for $n$ odd is a consequence of \cref{coro:neven}. Indeed, when ${\nu\leq -1}$, one has ${\ker D^+=0}$, and therefore $\mathcal{M}_{\nu,eq}^\infty(c_{n})=\varnothing$ when $c_{n}\neq0$; on the other hand, for $\nu=1$ the irreducible point $[(\sqrt{c_{n}/n}, 0,\ldots, 0), \Lambda_{E_{1}}]$, $c_n>0$, always belongs to $\mathcal{M}_{\nu,eq}^\infty(c_{n})$. For ${n}$ even, the symmetry is a consequence of \cref{XX} and \cref{nu2nu}.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{theo:compactmoduli}
    Let ${(G/K,\lambda{B_{{\mathfrak g}}}_{|_{{\mathfrak p}}}})$ be a $2n$-dimensional irreducible compact Hermitian symmetric space, $ {E_\nu}$ be a one-dimensional admissible twist and $ {A\in \mathcal{A}^G}$. The equivariant smooth solutions and moduli are given as follows.
\begin{align*}
{\mathcal{Z}_{\nu,eq}^\infty(c_{n}(t,\nu,\lambda))}\ &\simeq\
\begin{cases}
\text{the circle }{\{ |\psi^{(0)}|=\sqrt{c_{n}/n}\}\simeq \mathbb{S}^1}, & {c_{n}>0,\  \nu=1,}\\[2pt]
{\varnothing,}& {c_{n}>0,\  \nu\neq 1,}\\[2pt]
\text{the singleton } \{\psi=0\}, & {c_{n}=0,}\\[2pt]
{\varnothing}, &{c_{n}<0,\ (\nu\neq -1 \text{ or n odd} ),}\\[2pt]
    \text{the circle }{\{ |\psi^{(n)}|=\sqrt{|c_{n}|/n}\}\simeq \mathbb{S}^1}, &{c_{n}<0, \ }\nu=-1\text{, n even.} 
\end{cases}\\
{\mathcal{M}_{\nu,eq}^\infty(c_{n}(t,\nu,\lambda))}\ &\simeq\
\begin{cases}
{\{pt\},} & {c_{n}>0,\  \nu=1,}\\[2pt]
{\varnothing,} & {c_{n}>0,\ \nu\neq 1}\\[2pt]
{\{\text{reducible pt}\},} & {c_{n}=0,}\\[2pt]
{\varnothing,} &{c_{n}<0,\ (\nu\neq -1\text{ or n odd}),}\\[2pt]
{\{pt\},} &{c_{n}<0, \ \nu=-1,\ \text{n even}.}
\end{cases}
\end{align*}
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
According to Theorems 3 and 4 of \cite{La00} and \cref{bott}
\[\ker D^{+}(\mathcal{E}_{\nu})=\bigoplus_{q\ \mathrm{even}}H^{(0,q)}\bigl(G/K,\mathcal{E}_{(\nu-1)\rho_{{\mathfrak p}}}\bigr).\]
By Theorem IV of \cite{Bo57}, \cref{weylelem} and \cref{exeptweylelem}, the kernel has at most one non-zero summand, and the degree is forced to be $q\in\{0,n\}$. Suppose $\psi$ is concentrated in degree $0$ and $c_{n}\ne0$. By \cref{geeii}, for the $\eta_{ij}$, $\theta_{ij}$-conditions, $\gamma(\eta_{ij})$, $\gamma(\theta_{ij})$ shift exterior degree by $\pm2$; since $ \psi$ is concentrated in a single degree, the pairings vanish automatically. The first equation of
\cref{theo:monopole} reads 
\[n\,|\psi^{(0)}|^{2}=c_{n}, \qquad\text{so }c_{n}>0\text{ and }|\psi^{(0)}|\text{ is pointwise constant.}\] 
By \cref{uweights}, the degree-zero component is a section of $\mathcal{E}_{\nu-1}$, so \cref{cor:muzero}, gives $\nu=1$. The solutions form the circle of radius $\sqrt{c_{n}/n}$, on which $\mathcal{G}_{eq}\simeq U(1)$ acts simply transitively. Suppose now that $\psi$ is concentrated in degree $n$. This requires $n$ even, since otherwise the summand lies in $S^{-}$ and $\ker D^{+}=0$ by \cref{coro:neven}. Applying \cref{hodgeserre} and \cref{theo:parity} reduces this case to the previous one with $c_{n}$ replaced by $-c_{n}$ and $\nu$ by $-\nu$, giving $\nu=-1$, $c_{n}<0$ and $|\psi^{(n)}|=\sqrt{|c_{n}|/n}$. Finally, if $c_{n}=0$ then in either concentration degree the first equation forces $\psi=0$, and the invariant connection $\Lambda_{E_{\nu}}$ is unconstrained.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- corollary-9: body_md -->
\label{cor:injection}
The quadratic map $\mathcal{Q}$ induces an injection $\mathcal{M}^{\infty}_{\nu,eq}(c_{n})\hookrightarrow \mathcal{X}_{n}(c_{n})$, whose image is a single point in the Veronese cone whenever the source is non-empty.
<!-- end corollary-9 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{ZM2}
    Let ${(G/K,\lambda{B_{{\mathfrak g}}}_{|_{{\mathfrak p}}}})$ be a $2n$-dimensional irreducible non-compact Hermitian symmetric space, $ {E_\nu}$ be a one-dimensional admissible twist and $ {A\in \mathcal{A}^G}$. The equivariant solutions and moduli are given as follows.
\begin{align*}
{\mathcal{Z}_{\nu,eq}^{L^2}(c_{n})}\ &\simeq\
\begin{cases}
\varnothing, & {c_{n}\neq 0,}\\[2pt]
\text{the singleton } \{\psi=0\}, & {c_{n}=0.}        
                                  
\end{cases}    \\
{\mathcal{M}_{\nu,eq}^{L^2}(c_{n})}\ &\simeq\
\begin{cases}
{\varnothing,} & \hspace{12mm}  {c_{n}\neq0,}\\[2pt]
{\{\text{reducible pt}\},} & \hspace{12mm} {c_{n}=0.}
                                  
\end{cases}
\end{align*}
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
By Theorem 9.3 of \cite{AS77} the $L^{2}$-kernel is again concentrated in degree $0$ or $n$. If $c_{n}\ne0$, the first equation of \cref{theo:monopole} forces $|\psi|^{2}$ to be a non-zero constant function, hence $\|\psi\|_{L^{2}}=\infty$ on a space of infinite volume, which is a contradiction. Therefore, $c_{n}=0$, and then $|\psi|=0$.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
In the non-compact case, there exist equivariant solutions which are smooth but not ${L^2}$. For such solutions, $\psi$ lies in ${\ker_{C^{\infty}}D^+}$ but outside the discrete-series realisation ${\ker_{L^2}D^+}$, and the compact finite-energy variational argument does not apply.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
Let ${(G/K,\lambda{B_{{\mathfrak g}}}_{|_{{\mathfrak p}}}})$ be a $2n$-dimensional irreducible compact Hermitian symmetric space. If                                                                                                           
    ${(\mathcal{M}_\nu^\infty(c_n))^G}$ denotes the fixed-point locus of the ${G}$-action,
\begin{equation}\label{eqequalG}
    {(\mathcal{M}_\nu^\infty(c_n))^G=\mathcal{M}_{\nu,eq}^\infty(c_n)}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
If ${[\psi,A]}$ is fixed by $G$, then $F_A$ is $G$-invariant. We average $A$ over the compact group $G$. The averaged connection is $G$-invariant and has the same curvature, because $F_A$ is already invariant. Hence, the difference between the two connections is a closed $i\mathbb{R}$-valued one-form. Since 
    \[H^1(G/K,\mathbb{R}) =0\]
    for compact irreducible Hermitian symmetric spaces, this difference is removed by a gauge transformation. Thus, the gauge class has a representative with $A\in A^G$. For such a representative, fixedness of the class gives, for each $g\in G$, a gauge transformation $u_g$ with $g^*\psi = u_g\psi$. Because $A$ is $G$-invariant, \cref{prop:gaugeeq} implies that $u_g$ is constant on $G/K$. If $\psi\neq0$ the cocycle relation makes $g\mapsto u_g$ a continuous character of $G$. Since $G$ is connected and simple, this character is trivial. Hence $g^*\psi = \psi$ for all $g$. If $\psi=0$, the conclusion is immediate. The reverse inclusion is immediate from \cref{theo:compactmoduli}.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{equivreg}
    Let $M=G/K$ be compact irreducible, let $E_\nu$ be a one-dimensional admissible twist and let $\mu= \deg_\omega(\mathcal{E}_{\nu-1})$, $\nu\geq 1$. Then
   \begin{equation}
 \left(\mathcal{M}_\nu^\infty(c_{n})\right)^G\cong
 \begin{cases}
   \left(\ensuremath{\mathrm{Div}\,}_+^{\mu}(M)\right)^G,&c_{n}>0,\\
   \left(\ensuremath{\mathrm{Hol}\,}^{\mu}(M)\right)^G,&c_{n}=0,\\
   \varnothing,&c_{n}<0.
 \end{cases}
 \end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
On a Hermitian symmetric space there are no non-zero effective $G$-invariant divisors, so $(\ensuremath{\mathrm{Div}\,}_+^{\mu}(M))^{G}$ $=\varnothing$ for every $\mu>0$, equivalently $\nu>1$. The case $\mu=0$, equivalently $\nu=1$, describes the zero divisor which corresponds to the nowhere-vanishing section of \cref{theo:compactmoduli}. For $c_{n}=0$, the $G$-equivariant holomorphic line bundles are parametrised by $\nu$ as in \cref{1-1cor} and the same holds for the reducible points of \cref{theo:compactmoduli}.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
For $\nu\leq -1$ and $n$ even, \cref{theo:parity} identifies the moduli at $(c_n,\nu)$ with those at $(-c_n,-\nu)$, so the negative branch is the Serre-dual copy of the same trichotomy with $\mu=\deg_\omega(\mathcal{E}_{-\nu-1})$. For $n$ odd, it is empty by \cref{coro:neven}.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
